claims.text: Systematic variation of elemental percentages in HfNbTaTiZr will produce measurable changes in mechanical properties.
The mechanical-property changes will arise from altered lattice distortion and phase stability.
The initial equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase.
The initial alloy can be produced by conventional casting or sputtering.
High-throughput combinatorial synthesis combined with design of experiments can be used to vary one or more constituent percentages.
Applying identical thermal treatment and room-temperature testing will help isolate composition effects.
Changes in elemental concentration modify lattice distortion.
Changes in elemental concentration can alter grain size.
Changes in elemental concentration can cause secondary-phase formation.
Changing the relative amounts of the constituent elements changes the degree of solid-solution strengthening.
Composition changes may alter dislocation mobility.
Changes in solid-solution strengthening and dislocation mobility alter yield strength and hardness.
Increasing Hf or Ta beyond the equiatomic ratio is expected to increase strength and hardness through increased lattice distortion.
Some compositional adjustments may reduce ductility.
Exceeding the single-phase composition region may cause phase separation or secondary-phase formation.
Secondary phases complicate the alloy's mechanical behavior.
The magnitude and nonlinearity of property changes depend on processing conditions and interactions among strengthening mechanisms.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome includes phase separation after leaving the single-phase region, while the boundary says the predictions are valid only within the single-phase regime. This is a scope inconsistency rather than a direct physical contradiction.
